title: Maryland lawmakers ‘disheartened’ by persistent inequities in Black maternal health outcomes
summary: Persistent inequities in Black maternal health outcomes 'dishearten' Maryland lawmakers
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters February 13, 2026

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters February 13, 2026

Del. Jennifer White Holland (D-Baltimore County) said she has a new “anchor” to her work as a legislator pushing to improve maternal health outcomes — her name is Ryleigh, the delegate’s 6-month-old daughter.

Juggling diaper changes for her “deputy delegate” and her legislative duties is giving White Holland firsthand working mom experience. But it was moving through the medical system as a Black pregnant woman that showed her how much still needs to be done to improve health care for mothers in Maryland — specifically Black mothers.

“As I speak to other moms, it is, ‘Am I heard? … Am I being listened to? Am I being cared for differently than others?’” she said. “Having to signal that I am well-informed and deserve to be treated with the utmost respect and ensuring that I’m receiving the care that is needed and is deserved.”

White Holland said that experience will help guide her in another new role — chair of a new subcommittee focusing on maternal health.

She’s not alone in wanting changes. Several members of the House Health Committee recently pressed state health officials on a lack of progress in bettering maternal health outcomes for Black women, which continuously falls behind women of other races and ethnicities.

During the informational briefing, Maryland’s Deputy Director of Public Health Services Meg Sullivan agreed that while the health department attempts to improve maternal health across the state, there’s still significant work to do.

“We continue to see unacceptable disparities in maternal outcomes that are multifaceted and systemic — particularly for Black women and families facing structural barriers, like limited access to care, economic instability and geographic isolation,” Sullivan told lawmakers.

Noelene K. Jeffers, an assistant professor with Johns Hopkins School of Nursing who also has 10 years of experience as a nurse-midwife, said that disparities in Black maternal health are present across the United States, and have been a problem for decades.

“Racism is a source of chronic stress for Black women and long-term exposure to it … creates a physiologic stress response from the body,” she said. “It also impacts how you are able to access care and how you’re able to experience care. “

She said that there are also challenges in equitable access to adequate health care, whether it’s proximity to high-quality hospitals, access to green space for regular exercise, or living in a food desert.

“All of these impact how someone is able to access care. And it impacts the care that they receive as well,” Jeffers said, adding that there may be “underlying bias that providers may have against Black women and other women of color.

“It may impact how likely they are to listen when someone has a concern,” she said. “How likely are they to make sure that patients get timely care … to make sure that problems are caught early and not allowed to escalate.”

Such disparities in care may be deadly, as Maryland data shows Black mothers face a higher rate of maternal mortality.

From 2019 through 2023, Maryland had a maternal mortality rate of 21 per 100,000 births across all races and ethnicities, according to data from the Maryland Department of Health. But for Black mothers the mortality rate waa 30 deaths per 100,000 live births.

Another point of concern is the rate of “low-risk” births that result in cesarean section.

Maryland has the highest rate of C-sections on low-risk births compared to the rest of the nation, according to America’s Health Rankings data. In Maryland, 30.3% of low-risk births were delivered by C-section in 2023. Meanwhile, the national average was 26.6% for that year.

Jeffers emphasized that C-sections can be lifesaving. But they also carry higher risks than vaginal births, so it’s important to ensure that health care providers reduce the rate of what could be unnecessary C-sections. She said the percent of C-sections for low-risk births is a “signal” for researchers and policymakers to look into the data further.

“What we know is that these births are happening among women who have been defined as ‘low-risk,’” Jeffers said. “It’s their first time giving birth, they’re giving birth full-term … and the baby’s head is down.

“Just like any surgery, cesarean sections come with their risks. There’s a higher risk of hemorrhage, there’s a higher risk to other organs – like the bladder, the bowel. There’s a higher risk of infection. These can be serious,” she said. “It can also increase the risk for future surgeries as well.”

State data from the March of Dimes shows that Black Marylanders are more likely to have low-risk cesarean births than white, Asian and Native American mothers.

The data reports that from 2021-2023, the average low risk cesarean rate for Black women was 34.8, compared to the state average of 30.3, though Asian/Pacific Islanders fall closely behind at 32.

“This is a … data set that is really hard to look at,” Sullivan told lawmakers. “And the team is really trying to unpack what some of those contributing factors are — which we know are both at the health care facility and the provider level, as well as some contributions related to risk factors during pregnancy.”

But many members of the Health Committee are tired of seeing the data and want to see improvements.

During the committee meeting Del. Tiffany Alston (D-Prince George’s) expressed frustration that the department’s briefing was “not necessarily new information.” Health Committee Vice Chair Bonnie Cullison (D-Montgomery) added she was “a little disheartened … that we still have these really high levels, and particularly racial inequities and disparities in the outcomes.”

White Holland told Sullivan that it was concerning to see the “stark inequities … as someone who sees themselves in the data — who is living this in real time.”

As chair of the Maternal, Childhood and Infant Health Subcommittee, White Holland wants to target some of the ongoing challenges in the health care system that creates disparities in outcomes for mothers of different backgrounds.

She also plans to have the subcommittee look at external factors that may not be as obviously related to the health and wellbeing of pregnant women that can affect maternal health long before a pregnancy begins — such as access to nutritious food and other environmental factors.

“Naming this as a subcommittee alone illustrates our commitment as a legislature in prioritizing this issue,” she said.

“Having it as a standalone allows us to really hone in on this issue and to be more intentional about the partnerships we have, the connections we make and the types of interventions we put forth — and how we really hold our institutions accountable for the type of outcomes that we are seeing,” she said.
